content.rendered:
You could argue who did it better, The Drifters or Dion and The Belmonts, but either way you’d be right.

Written by the great songwriting team of Lieber and Stoller, “Ruby Baby” rocks, swings, saunters, and steamrolls in both versions.

The Drifters came first, releasing their original track in 1956 and notching a #10 berth on the Billboard R&B chart.

Dion’s 1963 version did even better, peaking at #5 on the R&B chart and all the way at #2 on the Top 100.

As for which version of “Ruby Baby” influenced Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band on the only two occasions they performed it, you could once again fairly argue for both.

Bruce and the band debuted “Ruby Baby” at one of their legendary surprise gigs at The Stone Pony on a Sunday night in August 1987. Listen to their performance below, and you’ll clearly hear the “hey hey!” from Dion’s arrangement as well as Clarence’s smoking sax solo tribute to the Drifters’ original.

Exactly one week later, they took another run at it–but this time in a slower, steamier arrangement that draws on both influences and grounds them on E Street.

Although neither recording is as clear as we’d like, it’s still easy to hear just how much fun the band has with the classic R&B track–why this one hasn’t shown up in Bruce’s set lists since is hard to fathom.

Ruby Baby
First performed: August 2, 1987 (Asbury Park, NJ)
Last performed: August 9, 1987 (Asbury Park, NJ)

© January 14, 2020

excerpt.rendered: Twice only: Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band turn in steamy performances of “Ruby Baby” at The Stone Pony in the summer of 1987.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Up on the Roof
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: For a brief time during the summer of 1975, Bruce's shows featured a sweet, tender cover of The Drifters' "Up on the Roof."

jetpack-related-posts.title: Cover Me, Southside Johnny (and The Drifters!): Little Girl So Fine
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Now here's a recipe: Start with inspiration from Leiber and Staller, add lyrics by Bruce, music by Steve, and lead vocals by Southside Johnny. Ice with backing vocals by The Drifters, and you've got pure pop confection.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Come on Over to My Place
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Drifters' classic makes frequent appearances at the Stone Pony in 1982.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Under the Boardwalk
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Bruce and Bobby cover "Under the Boardwalk" on the Jersey Shore on the third day of summer. There's no setting more perfect for that song.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Roll of the Dice: The Brokenhearted
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: "The Brokenhearted" is Roy Orbison meets The Drifters, and 1977 Bruce meets 2010 Bruce. The style mash-up works, the vocal graft not so much.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Roll of the Dice/Cover Me, Clarence Clemons: Savin’ Up
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Double-entry today: "Savin' Up" is a Bruce Springsteen original composition, recorded by Clarence Clemons and the Red Bank Rockers, but performed live by Bruce on many occasions.
